title: SQL Basics — DDL & DML
summary: Covers SQL fundamentals: Data Definition Language (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), Data Manipulation Language (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), basic SELECT-FROM-WHERE queries, data types, and constraints.

definitions.definition: SQL commands that define/modify the database structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP.
definitions.example: CREATE TABLE Student(ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(50));

definitions.definition: SQL commands that manipulate data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT.
definitions.example: INSERT INTO Student VALUES (1, 'Ahmad');

definitions.definition: A constraint that uniquely identifies each row. Cannot be NULL. Only ONE per table.
definitions.example: CREATE TABLE T(id INT PRIMARY KEY);

definitions.definition: A constraint that ensures referential integrity between tables. References a primary key in another table.
definitions.example: FOREIGN KEY (DeptID) REFERENCES Department(ID);

definitions.definition: A constraint that prevents NULL values in a column.
definitions.example: Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL

definitions.definition: A constraint that ensures all values in a column are different. Unlike PK, a table can have multiple UNIQUE columns.
definitions.example: Email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE

definitions.definition: A constraint that limits the values that can be placed in a column.
definitions.example: CHECK (Age >= 18)

definitions.definition: Used to add, delete, or modify columns and constraints in an existing table.
definitions.example: ALTER TABLE Student ADD Email VARCHAR(100);

definitions.definition: VARCHAR(n) stores variable-length strings (saves space). CHAR(n) stores fixed-length strings (padded with spaces).
definitions.example: VARCHAR(20) with 'Avi' uses 3 spaces. CHAR(20) with 'Avi' uses 20 spaces.

mustKnowConcepts.title: SELECT-FROM-WHERE Structure
mustKnowConcepts.description: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition. SELECT and FROM are mandatory. WHERE is optional. Correct order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Composite Primary Key Syntax
mustKnowConcepts.description: For composite keys, use: PRIMARY KEY (col1, col2) as a table constraint, not inline.

mustKnowConcepts.title: DELETE vs DROP vs TRUNCATE
mustKnowConcepts.description: DELETE FROM table: removes rows (can use WHERE). DROP TABLE: removes entire table structure. DELETE FROM table (no WHERE): clears all rows but keeps structure.

mustKnowConcepts.title: DDL vs DML Classification
mustKnowConcepts.description: DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP (schema changes). DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT (data changes). TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK. DCL: GRANT, REVOKE.

mustKnowConcepts.title: WHERE Clause is Critical with DELETE
mustKnowConcepts.description: DELETE without WHERE deletes ALL records. Always use WHERE to target specific rows.

mustKnowConcepts.title: NULL Comparison
mustKnowConcepts.description: Cannot use = or != with NULL. Must use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. Comparing with = NULL yields UNKNOWN, not TRUE.

examTricks.trick: Correct keyword order: SELECT → FROM → WHERE (not SELECT → WHERE → FROM)
examTricks.explanation: This is tested frequently. The order matters in SQL syntax.

examTricks.trick: INSERT is DML, ALTER is DDL — don't mix them up
examTricks.explanation: INSERT manipulates data. ALTER changes table structure.

examTricks.trick: A table can have only ONE primary key but MULTIPLE unique constraints
examTricks.explanation: Primary key = unique + not null. Only one allowed per table.

examTricks.trick: VARCHAR(20) with 'Avi' has 3 spaces, CHAR(20) has 20 spaces
examTricks.explanation: This exact question appeared in the 2021 exam. VARCHAR = variable length, CHAR = fixed.

examTricks.trick: To add a row use INSERT, not ADD/CREATE/MAKE
examTricks.explanation: INSERT INTO table VALUES(...); is the correct syntax.

confusedConcepts.difference: DELETE removes rows from a table (DML, table still exists). DROP removes the entire table structure (DDL).
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: DELETE = erasing text from a page. DROP = throwing away the entire page.

confusedConcepts.difference: WHERE filters individual rows BEFORE grouping. HAVING filters groups AFTER aggregation with GROUP BY.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: WHERE = bouncer at the door. HAVING = judge after the competition.

confusedConcepts.difference: PK: unique + not null + only one per table. UNIQUE: unique but allows NULL + multiple per table.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: PK = national ID (one per person, mandatory). UNIQUE = phone number (unique but optional).

keyPoints: PRIMARY KEY (unique + not null, one per table)

title: SQL Aggregation & Functions
summary: Covers aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN), GROUP BY clause, HAVING clause, NULL handling in aggregates, and UPDATE with conditions.

definitions.definition: Functions that take a collection of values as input and return a single value. The five built-in: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN.
definitions.example: SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(Salary) FROM Employee;

definitions.definition: Groups rows that share a value into summary rows. Used with aggregate functions to compute per-group statistics.
definitions.example: SELECT Dept, AVG(Salary) FROM Emp GROUP BY Dept;

definitions.definition: Filters groups after aggregation. Similar to WHERE but used for aggregate conditions. Must be used with GROUP BY.
definitions.example: SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM Emp GROUP BY Dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

definitions.definition: Counts all rows including NULLs. COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values only.
definitions.example: COUNT(*) returns total rows. COUNT(Salary) skips NULL salaries.

definitions.definition: AVG() ignores NULL values — it only averages non-NULL values.
definitions.example: If salaries are 100, NULL, 200: AVG = 150 (not 100).

mustKnowConcepts.title: Five Built-in Aggregate Functions
mustKnowConcepts.description: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN. This exact set is tested frequently. Not MULT, DIV, NUMBER, or NAME.

mustKnowConcepts.title: GROUP BY + HAVING Order
mustKnowConcepts.description: Correct order: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY. HAVING comes AFTER GROUP BY, never before.

mustKnowConcepts.title: HAVING vs WHERE
mustKnowConcepts.description: WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping. HAVING filters groups AFTER aggregation. HAVING is similar to WHERE but used for groups rather than rows.

mustKnowConcepts.title: NULL Handling in Aggregates
mustKnowConcepts.description: All aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, etc.) ignore NULL values. COUNT(*) counts all rows. COUNT(col) skips NULLs.

mustKnowConcepts.title: AVG Salary Query Pattern
mustKnowConcepts.description: SELECT branch_name, AVG(amount) FROM loan GROUP BY branch_name; — must include GROUP BY when selecting non-aggregate with aggregate.

examTricks.trick: HAVING cannot be used without GROUP BY — it's specifically for filtering groups
examTricks.explanation: HAVING clause must be used with GROUP BY. It cannot be used for pattern matching like LIKE.

examTricks.trick: The five built-in functions are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN — not MULT or NUMBER
examTricks.explanation: This specific list appears in exams. Wrong options often include MULT, DIV, NUMBER, NAME.

examTricks.trick: SELECT Dept, SUM(Salary) FROM Emp HAVING SUM(Salary)>5000 GROUP BY Dept is WRONG order
examTricks.explanation: HAVING must come AFTER GROUP BY. Correct: ...GROUP BY Dept HAVING SUM(Salary) > 5000;

examTricks.trick: To find mean salary use AVG(salary), not Mean(salary)
examTricks.explanation: SQL has no Mean() function. Use AVG(). Also Sum(salary)/Count(salary) works but Count(staff_ID) doesn't.

examTricks.trick: Finding largest loan per branch: SELECT branch_name, MAX(amount) FROM loan GROUP BY branch_name
examTricks.explanation: Must GROUP BY branch_name. Cannot use WHERE amount = MAX(amount) directly.

confusedConcepts.difference: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters grouped results after aggregation.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: WHERE = filtering ingredients before cooking. HAVING = tasting the final dish.

confusedConcepts.difference: COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs. COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values in that column.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: COUNT(*) = counting all seats. COUNT(person) = counting occupied seats only.

keyPoints: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
AVG per group: SELECT col, AVG(x) FROM t GROUP BY col
Filter groups: add HAVING after GROUP BY
Find max per group: MAX(col) with GROUP BY

title: SQL Joins & Set Operations
summary: Covers JOIN types (INNER, LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER, NATURAL, CROSS), set operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT/MINUS), and self-joins.

definitions.definition: Returns only rows where there is a match in BOTH tables. This is the SQL Server default join type.
definitions.example: SELECT * FROM A INNER JOIN B ON A.id = B.id;

definitions.definition: Returns ALL rows from the left table and matching rows from the right. Non-matching right rows show NULL.
definitions.example: SELECT * FROM Emp LEFT JOIN Dept ON Emp.DeptID = Dept.ID;

definitions.definition: Returns ALL rows from the right table and matching rows from the left. Non-matching left rows show NULL.
definitions.example: SELECT * FROM Emp RIGHT JOIN Dept ON Emp.DeptID = Dept.ID;

definitions.definition: Returns ALL rows from both tables. NULLs where there's no match on either side.
definitions.example: SELECT * FROM A FULL OUTER JOIN B ON A.id = B.id;

definitions.definition: Automatically joins tables using columns with the same name in both tables. No ON clause needed.
definitions.example: SELECT * FROM Emp NATURAL JOIN Dept;

definitions.definition: Returns every combination of rows from both tables. No join condition. Result size = rows_A × rows_B.
definitions.example: SELECT * FROM A CROSS JOIN B; — if A has 3 rows and B has 4, result has 12 rows.

definitions.definition: Combines results of two queries, removing duplicates. Both queries must have same number of columns and compatible types.
definitions.example: SELECT name FROM Students UNION SELECT name FROM Teachers;

definitions.definition: Returns only rows that appear in BOTH query results.
definitions.example: SELECT id FROM A INTERSECT SELECT id FROM B;

definitions.definition: Returns rows in the first query that are NOT in the second. Note: set difference is NOT commutative (A-B ≠ B-A).
definitions.example: SELECT id FROM A EXCEPT SELECT id FROM B;

definitions.definition: A table joined with itself, typically using aliases. Used for hierarchical data.
definitions.example: SELECT E1.Name, E2.Name as Manager FROM Emp E1 JOIN Emp E2 ON E1.ManagerID = E2.ID;

mustKnowConcepts.title: INNER JOIN is Default
mustKnowConcepts.description: In SQL Server, INNER JOIN is the default join type. If you write just JOIN, it means INNER JOIN.

mustKnowConcepts.title: SEMI JOIN is NOT Standard SQL
mustKnowConcepts.description: INNER, LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER, CROSS, NATURAL are standard SQL. SEMI JOIN is not an explicit SQL command.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Union Compatibility
mustKnowConcepts.description: For UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT: both queries must have same number of columns and compatible data types.

mustKnowConcepts.title: INNER JOIN Returns Only Matches
mustKnowConcepts.description: INNER JOIN only returns rows where the join condition matches in BOTH tables. No NULLs from non-matches.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Set Difference is NOT Commutative
mustKnowConcepts.description: A EXCEPT B ≠ B EXCEPT A. UNION and INTERSECT are commutative. Difference/EXCEPT is not.

examTricks.trick: SEMI JOIN is NOT a type of standard SQL join
examTricks.explanation: When asked 'which is NOT a join type', SEMI JOIN is the answer. It exists conceptually but not as SQL syntax.

examTricks.trick: Finding customers with loans: use JOIN between borrower and loan tables, not depositor and account
examTricks.explanation: Read the question carefully — loans vs deposits use different tables.
% = any characters. _ = single character. '%le%' finds 'angle', 'element', etc.

examTricks.trick: INNER join vs OUTER join: INNER = only matches, OUTER = all from one/both sides
examTricks.explanation: LEFT OUTER includes ALL left rows. RIGHT OUTER includes ALL right rows.

confusedConcepts.difference: INNER: only matching rows. OUTER: all rows from one or both sides, NULLs for non-matches.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: INNER = only those invited who showed up. OUTER = everyone invited even if they didn't show.

confusedConcepts.difference: UNION combines rows vertically (stacks results). JOIN combines columns horizontally (merges tables).
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: UNION = stacking papers on top of each other. JOIN = stapling papers side by side.

confusedConcepts.difference: CROSS: every possible pair (no condition). NATURAL: automatic match on same-named columns.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: CROSS = blind matching everyone. NATURAL = matching by shared interests.

keyPoints: LEFT OUTER: all left + matching right
RIGHT OUTER: all right + matching left
FULL OUTER: all from both sides
EXCEPT/MINUS: in first but not second
UNION needs same column count & types
SEMI JOIN is not standard SQL
INNER JOIN is SQL Server default
